We need the smallest $n$ with $P(n) = \prod_{k=1}^{n-1} k! > (n!)^2$. Compute both sides directly for small $n$.

| $n$ | $P(n)=\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}k!$ | $(n!)^2$ | $P(n)>(n!)^2$? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $1$ (empty product) | $1$ | No |
| 2 | $1$ | $4$ | No |
| 3 | $1\cdot 2 = 2$ | $36$ | No |
| 4 | $2\cdot 6 = 12$ | $576$ | No |
| 5 | $12\cdot 24 = 288$ | $14400$ | No |
| 6 | $288\cdot 120 = 34560$ | $518400$ | No |
| 7 | $34560\cdot 720 = 24883200$ | $5040^2 = 25401600$ | No |
| 8 | $24883200\cdot 5040 = 125411328000$ | $40320^2 = 1625702400$ | Yes |

For $n=7$ the product is $24{,}883{,}200 < 25{,}401{,}600$, so the inequality fails. For $n=8$ it holds by a wide margin.

Since $P(n)$ grows much faster than $(n!)^2$ from this point on, the inequality continues to hold for $n \ge 8$, but the question only asks for the smallest such $n$.

ANSWER: 8
